schools.summary: Gill reports the plain fact of Achish's gift of Ziklag.
Keil and Delitzsch map the chapter's two registers and gloss the archers' Hebrew; Ellicott traces Ziklag's tenure and the obscure clause about keeping close.
Henry reads David's concealment as the moment Providence was gathering helpers for him.
Clarke dates the gift of Ziklag; Wesley ascribes the Benjamites' coming to God's Spirit and their own conscience.

debates.question: What moved Saul's own tribesmen to come over to David?

sides.position: A generous indignation at the base treatment Saul had given David
God's Spirit, the conscience of duty to David, and the observation that God had left Saul

1.pericope_label: The Benjamites who came to David at Ziklag

schools.summary: Gill draws out that Gibeah was Saul's birthplace, so these men may be his kindred.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott work through the chiefs' titles, place-names and Hebrew text variants.
Wesley takes 'over the thirty' as a command of thirty Benjamites who came with Ishmaiah.

debates.question: What does 'over the thirty' say about Ishmaiah?

sides.position: Either he was once captain of the famous corps, or the phrase is merely comparative
He arrived attended by thirty valiant Benjamites and was their commander

3.pericope_label: The named chiefs of the Benjamite company

schools.summary: Gill denies the Korhites were Levites and makes them the posterity of a Benjaminite Korah.
Keil and Delitzsch argue the Levitical descent from the porters of the tabernacle; Ellicott weighs Levitical against Judean Korah and dates the mountain hold.

debates.question: Who were the Korhites in this company?

sides.position: Descendants of the Levite Korah, drawn from the porters of the holy place
Not Levites at all, but the posterity of a Korah of Benjamin
Members of the Levitical clan Korah, though possibly of the otherwise unknown Judean clan

debates.question: Why do Judaean names stand in a list of Benjamites?

sides.position: The chronicler welded two lists into one
Towns changed hands, so Judaean towns may have held a partly Benjaminite population
Gedor may have passed to Benjamin, or be another town of the same name

themes: Judaean names in a Benjamite list
6.pericope_label: The Korhites and the sons of Jeroham of Gedor

schools.summary: Gill describes what the Gadites separated themselves from and names the eleven in order.
Henry calls the separation laudable and contrasts these men with the distressed recruits of earlier days.
Clarke notes that speed was reckoned a grand accomplishment in a warrior.
Ellicott takes the description apart term by term and hears an ancient poetic source behind the lion-and-gazelle clause; Keil and Delitzsch read the subscription as marking chief warriors.

debates.question: Which stronghold was the hold in the wilderness?

sides.position: A hold in the wilderness of Ziph or Maon, or else Ziklag
Perhaps Adullam, Hachilah, Maon or En-gedi
Probably one of the holds in the wilderness of En-gedi

themes: lion faces and the swiftness of roes
8.pericope_label: The Gadites who separated themselves to the hold

schools.summary: Gill makes the captains officers of the militia at home and notes the crossing of Jordan.
Ellicott prefers the margin and calls the clause poetic; Keil and Delitzsch rest the same reading on the Hebrew preposition.
Clarke dates the first month and weighs two readings of the flood.
Henry has them officers who could command thousands, and daring men who swam the flooded river.

debates.question: Does 'one of the least was over an hundred' describe rank or prowess?

sides.position: Rank: the least commanded a hundred, the greatest a thousand
holders: the Syriac and Vulgate (as reported by Ellicott)

sides.position: Prowess: the weaker could cope with a hundred, the stronger with a thousand
holders: Bertheau (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

14.pericope_label: Captains of the host who crossed a flooded Jordan

schools.summary: Gill holds open both deference and suspicion as reasons for David going out to them.
Keil and Delitzsch account for the missing names; Ellicott glosses the terms of David's challenge clause by clause.
Henry reads the speech as fair dealing and admires David's restraint in referring his cause to God.
Wesley expounds the appeal to the God of our fathers.

debates.question: Why did David go out to meet them?

sides.position: Either out of respect for men of eminence, or to sound them before admitting them
Out of a jealousy learned from the treachery of Ziph and Keilah

themes: Benjamin and Judah at the hold
appeal to the God of our fathers
16.pericope_label: Benjamin and Judah come, and David puts them to the test

schools.summary: Gill renders the verb as clothing and calls Amasai a sister’s son of David’s.
Clarke gives the Targum's paraphrase; Wesley ascribes heroical motions to God's Spirit.
Keil and Delitzsch supply the omitted divine name; Ellicott prints the answer as verse and weighs Amasai's identity and title.
Henry distinguishes a spirit of wisdom and resolution from a spirit of prophecy.

debates.question: What spirit came upon Amasai?

sides.position: A spirit of fortitude, strength and presence of mind
holders: the Targum (as reported by Gill and Clarke)

sides.position: The Spirit of God, the divine name omitted or fallen out of the text
Not a spirit of prophecy but of wisdom and resolution for the occasion

debates.question: Is Amasai the Amasa of the later history?

sides.position: Perhaps the Amasa son of Abigail
holders: the older commentators (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: Whether he is that Amasa does not appear

outliers.note: He presses a modern paraphrase into theology, arguing that enthusiasm for truth and right is itself a sort of divine possession.

themes: peace to thee and to thy helpers

schools.summary: Gill states plainly that men of Manasseh took David’s part.
Keil and Delitzsch set out the desertion idiom and the Philistine lords' reasoning; Ellicott glosses the phrases and raises an alternative reading.
Henry reads the march through Manasseh as a providential opportunity.
Wesley fixes the second company to the return from the Philistine camp.

debates.question: Should the text read 'they helped them not' or 'he helped them'?

sides.position: The received reading: David and his men did not help the Philistines
Possibly 'he helped them', a different vocalisation of the same verb

19.pericope_label: The Manassites who fell to David

schools.summary: Gill identifies the rovers as the Amalekites who sacked Ziklag.
Clarke's Targum and Wesley both take the host of God for an innumerable army.
Henry turns the daily accessions into a lesson on waiting for God's strength.
Ellicott proposes a wholly different rendering of the clause; Keil and Delitzsch defend the nearer antecedent and read the host of God by power rather than number.

debates.question: What is 'the band' David was helped against or over?

sides.position: The Amalekite band that had burnt Ziklag
holders: the Vulgate and Syriac (as reported by Ellicott)

sides.position: Not a band of enemies but the joint command of his own forces

debates.question: Who are the men said to have helped David?

sides.position: The Manassites just named
All the heroes listed from the first verse onward
holders: Bertheau (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

debates.question: Does 'like the host of God' measure numbers or quality?

sides.position: Power and spirit, not the count of warriors
A very numerous army, innumerable as the stars or angels
An antique idiom marking excellence by the divine standard

21.pericope_label: Help against the rovers, and a host like the host of God

schools.summary: Henry frames the section as the quota each tribe brought and explains why the nearest tribes brought fewest.
Clarke dates the muster after the death of Ish-bosheth; Wesley says Judah came in the name of the whole tribe.
Gill glosses the armed bands as men trained and accounted fit for war.
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both refuse the Vulgate’s "chiefs of the army" and argue for companies or totals.

debates.question: What does the heading's word for 'heads' denote?

sides.position: Companies or bands of soldiers, that is, totals
Chiefs or leaders of the army
holders: the Vulgate and Septuagint (as reported by Ellicott)
Bertheau (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch)

sides.position: Polls, that is, individuals

themes: according to the word of the LORD
23.pericope_label: The muster at Hebron, and the men of Judah

schools.summary: Ellicott corrects the rendering of the military formula and explains how a tribe of priests came to muster.
Henry reads the Levites’ presence as conviction that David was called of God.

debates.question: Are Jehoiada's 3,700 inside Levi's 4,600?

sides.position: Probably not; the two figures stand beside each other

outliers.note: He reaches for a medieval comparison, likening these martial Levites to the priestly warriors of the crusades.

themes: the Levite as a tribal name

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both insist the title is princely rather than priestly, and measure the strength of Eleazar's house.
Clarke and Wesley place Jehoiada under Abiathar as captain of the warriors of Aaron.

27.pericope_label: Jehoiada the Aaronite leader, and Zadok

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch read the guard-keeping clause as the register's own explanation of Benjamin's small muster.
Wesley states the motive plainly as keeping the crown in Saul’s family.
Henry rebukes the tribal affection that kept Benjamin in a sinking interest.

debates.question: Why was Ephraim's contingent so small?

sides.position: The tribe was already declining within the Mosaic period
It had been greatly reduced by Saul's last wars with the Philistines

themes: keeping the ward of the house of Saul

schools.summary: Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both reject the astrological reading and restrict the praise to political sagacity.
Clarke relays the Targum’s astronomy; Wesley argues the political reading from the tribe’s conduct after Abner’s death.
Henry sets out three senses of knowing the times and prefers the political.

debates.question: What is Issachar's 'understanding of the times'?

sides.position: Astronomical and astrological skill in calendar and signs
holders: the old Jewish expositors (as reported by Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott)

sides.position: Knowing the right season for every matter and business
Political sagacity, and nothing more
Natural, ceremonial or, rather, political times

debates.question: Does the praise belong to the tribe or to its two hundred chiefs?

sides.position: To the two hundred heads only
The two hundred were in effect the whole tribe

themes: all their brethren at their commandment
31.pericope_label: Half Manasseh, and the men of Issachar who knew the times

schools.summary: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both derive the rare verb from the battle array rather than from helping, and compare the spear words.
Wesley reads the double heart as dissembling loyalty.
Henry singles Zebulun out as Israelites indeed, in whom was no guile.

debates.question: What does the verb rendered "could keep rank" mean?

sides.position: To help, as nine manuscripts and the Greek and Latin read it
holders: the Septuagint and Vulgate (as reported by Ellicott)

sides.position: To close up together, setting the battle array in order

themes: a rare verb for closing ranks
33.pericope_label: Zebulun, not of double heart, and Naphtali

schools.summary: Ellicott supplies the grammar of the tribal names, prefers the margin’s "rangers of battle", and declines to criticise the eastern total.

themes: from the other side of Jordan
35.pericope_label: Dan, Asher and the tribes beyond Jordan

schools.summary: Ellicott re-translates the subscription, moves its pause, counts the muster at over three hundred thousand and rebuts Reuss.
Gill glosses keeping rank as discipline.
Henry makes the perfect heart and the one heart the point of the whole muster.
Clarke argues that only the deputies can have feasted, and closes with a panegyric on David.

debates.question: Are the relative tribal numbers credible?

sides.position: It is absolutely inconceivable that the nearer tribes furnished so little
A hasty and uncritical exaggeration; we know too little of the tribes to judge

outliers.note: He breaks off into a panegyric, calling David unrivalled in the annals of the world as statesman, warrior, hero, poet and divine.

themes: the remainder of Israel of one heart
38.pericope_label: A perfect heart at Hebron, and three days of feasting

schools.summary: Gill limits "they that were nigh" to the neighbours of Hebron and Judah.
Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch widen the contributors to the northern tribes and gloss the beasts and the foodstuffs.
Henry reads the victualling as an equalising of charge and the joy as a figure of Christ enthroned in the soul.

outliers.note: He turns the three days of feasting into an argument for submitting to the Son of David, and closes with a call to ask God for wisdom.

40.pericope_label: Provisions from near and far, for there was joy in Israel
